title: Is the Four-Day Week Too Good to Be True?
subtitle: Artículo de opinión: argumentos a favor y en contra

paragraphs: Imagine finishing work on Thursday afternoon, every week, without losing a penny of your salary. For most of the twentieth century, the five-day, forty-hour week was treated as a law of nature, as fixed as the number of days in a week. Now, after a series of trials in several countries, a growing number of employers are asking a question that would once have seemed absurd: what if we worked one day less and got the same amount done?

The idea is not as new as it sounds. The weekend itself is a relatively recent invention. In the nineteenth century, factory workers in Britain often worked six days a week, and the two-day weekend only became common in the decades after the First World War. Each reduction in working hours was greeted with warnings that business would collapse. In each case, it didn't. Supporters of the four-day week argue that we are simply due for the next step.

The most widely reported experiment took place in Britain in 2022, when around sixty companies, from software developers to a fish and chip shop, agreed to give their staff a paid day off every week for six months. The model was known as "100-80-100": employees received 100 per cent of their pay for 80 per cent of their time, in exchange for a commitment to deliver 100 per cent of their usual output. When the trial ended, the vast majority of the companies chose to continue, and several made the change permanent. Earlier trials in the public sector in Iceland, involving thousands of workers, had reported similar results.

Supporters point to a long list of benefits. Employees in most trials reported feeling less stressed, sleeping better and having more time for their families, their hobbies and, crucially, the boring tasks of everyday life, such as going to the dentist, which otherwise eat into the weekend. Fewer people took sick days. Some companies found it easier to attract new staff, because a four-day week turned out to be a highly effective way of standing out in a competitive job market. "We used to lose good people to bigger firms that could pay more," one manager of a small design agency told me. "Now people apply to us precisely because of the extra day."

Perhaps more surprisingly, many employers claimed that productivity didn't fall. In some cases, they said, it actually rose. The explanation, according to researchers, is that a large part of the traditional working week is not particularly productive. Long meetings, constant email and endless interruptions take up hours that could be used for real work. When people know they have only four days, they tend to be ruthless about what really matters. Meetings get shorter. Unnecessary reports quietly disappear. "I'd always assumed I was busy," one accountant admitted. "It turned out I was just in a lot of meetings."

What does a four-day week look like in practice? At one small engineering firm in the Midlands, the change began with a month of preparation. Staff were asked to keep a diary of how they spent their time, and the results were sobering: the average employee was spending almost a day a week in meetings, many of which had no clear purpose. Meetings were limited to thirty minutes, internal emails were replaced by a single shared message board, and the office introduced two hours of "quiet time" every morning, during which nobody was allowed to interrupt anyone else. "The first few weeks were chaotic," the managing director admitted. "People were worried that customers would complain. In the end, only one did, and that was because he wanted to call us on a Friday afternoon to talk about football."

There is an environmental argument too. If millions of people stopped commuting one day a week, the reduction in traffic and energy use could be significant, at least in theory. Offices that close for an extra day need less heating and lighting. Critics point out, however, that people with an extra day off do not simply sit at home. They may drive to the coast, take more short-haul flights or go shopping, all of which have their own environmental costs. As with many of the claims made for the four-day week, the honest answer is that it depends on how people choose to use their time.

Sceptics, however, are not convinced, and their objections deserve to be taken seriously. The first is that the companies which volunteered for these trials were hardly a random sample. Firms that are enthusiastic about a four-day week are likely to be the ones best suited to it: small, flexible and mostly office-based. Whether the same results could be achieved in a hospital, a school or a factory is a very different question. A nurse cannot simply finish her shift early because she has been more efficient, and patients do not stop being ill on Fridays.

The second objection concerns what happens in the long run. A trial lasts a few months, and people who know they are being observed often work harder than usual. Psychologists have a name for this: the observer effect. Critics argue that once the novelty wears off, old habits may return. If productivity slowly falls, the company will be left paying the same salaries for less work, and a benefit that has been given is extremely difficult to take away. "Nobody has ever gone on strike to get a five-day week back," one economist pointed out.

There is also the question of who pays. In sectors where work cannot be compressed, such as care, transport or retail, giving everyone a day off means hiring more people, and someone has to pay for them. That someone might be the taxpayer, the customer or the employer, but it is unlikely to be nobody. For a small business operating on thin profit margins, an extra twenty per cent on the wage bill could make the difference between surviving and closing. Some economists also worry that a four-day week for office workers could widen the gap between those who sit at a desk and those who cannot.

Some researchers have raised a further point, which is rarely mentioned in the headlines. Many people already work four days a week, or fewer, but they do it part-time and are paid accordingly. A large proportion of them are parents, often mothers, who have reduced their hours to look after children. If full-time employees are suddenly given a paid day off, those part-time workers may reasonably ask why they are still earning less for the same hours. Any company that introduces a four-day week, these researchers argue, needs to think carefully about fairness, not just about productivity.

Finally, there are concerns about the days that remain. In some trials, employees reported that their four working days had become more intense, with fewer breaks and less time for the informal conversations that make a workplace enjoyable. "I love having Fridays off," one software engineer said, "but Monday to Thursday I barely have time to eat lunch." If the price of a long weekend is a working week in which every minute is measured, not everyone will think it is worth paying.

So where does that leave us? Most researchers agree that the evidence so far is encouraging but incomplete. What seems clear is that there is no single model that works for everyone. Some companies have chosen to close on Fridays; others keep the office open five days and give staff different days off. Some have reduced hours to thirty-two a week; others have compressed forty hours into four longer days, which is a rather different thing. Supporters argue that this flexibility is a strength. Critics see it as proof that the idea is still too vague to be applied across a whole economy.

It is also worth remembering that the debate is not only about efficiency. For many people, the question is not whether a four-day week makes companies richer, but whether it makes lives better. Had the trials shown a small fall in productivity, some argue, a society might still decide that the gain in health and happiness was worth it. Others reply that such choices are a luxury that only rich economies can afford. Both sides have a point, and the answer may depend less on the data than on what we believe work is for.

What would I do if I were running a company? Honestly, I'm not sure. If I'd been asked ten years ago, I would have dismissed the idea as a fantasy. Today, having read the results of the trials and spoken to people on both sides, I think it deserves a fair chance, at least in the kinds of jobs where it has been tested. But I would want to see what happens after five years, not five months, before declaring a revolution. The five-day week took decades to become normal. If the four-day week is going to replace it, it will probably take just as long, and that, perhaps, is no bad thing.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, what has happened every time working hours were reduced in the past?
options: People predicted disaster, but it didn't happen.
Businesses collapsed for a few years.
Workers asked for even shorter weeks.

questions.question: What does "100-80-100" mean?
options: Workers lose 20% of their pay but keep their output.
Full pay for less time, with the same output expected.
Companies produce 80% of their usual output.

questions.question: Why did one small agency find it easier to hire staff?
options: It started paying more than bigger firms.
Bigger firms stopped hiring.
The extra day off attracted people even though it couldn't pay more.

questions.question: According to researchers, why didn't productivity fall in many companies?
options: Time was previously wasted on things like long meetings and interruptions.
Employees worked longer hours on the remaining days.
Companies hired more staff.

questions.question: What is the problem with the companies that took part in the trials, according to sceptics?
options: They were chosen at random.
They were the type of companies most likely to succeed with the idea.
They were all very large.

questions.question: In paragraph 7, "the observer effect" refers to people…
options: refusing to take part in experiments.
watching their colleagues work.
working harder because they know they are being watched.

questions.question: What does the software engineer's comment illustrate?
options: The four working days can become more intense.
Engineers prefer a five-day week.
Lunch breaks are longer in a four-day week.

questions.question: What is the writer's final opinion?
options: The four-day week should be introduced everywhere now.
The idea deserves a chance, but long-term evidence is needed.
The idea is a fantasy that will never work.

exam_practice.title: Uso del inglés · Una palabra por hueco
exam_practice.instructions: Como en los exámenes oficiales: escribe una sola palabra en cada hueco.

items.text: The weekend, ___ only became common after the First World War, is a relatively recent invention. ___ trials suggest that productivity doesn't always fall, critics remain unconvinced.
items.hint: Oración explicativa entre comas: which (nunca that).

items.text: Some managers are used ___ losing staff to bigger firms. Employees tend to be ruthless about ___ really matters. Some had less time for ___ informal conversations that make a workplace enjoyable.
items.hint: Be used to + -ing: estar acostumbrado a. Con un nombre concretado por lo que sigue: the.

items.text: If I ___ running a company, I wouldn't be sure what to do. If I had been asked ten years ago, I would ___ dismissed the idea.
items.hint: Hipótesis presente: if + were. Pasada: would have + participio.

exam_practice.title: Formación de palabras
exam_practice.instructions: Escribe una palabra derivada de la que está entre paréntesis (por ejemplo, DECIDE → decision).

items.text: Companies promised to keep their usual ___ (PRODUCE). Some firms found the change ___ (HIGH) effective for hiring. The four-day week is becoming ___ (INCREASE) popular.
items.hint: Highly va con adjetivos como effective, successful.

items.text: Critics have strong ___ (OBJECT) to the idea. The trial results were ___ (ENCOURAGE) but incomplete. Many employees reported less ___ (STRESSED).
items.hint: Plural tras strong. Stress es el nombre.

exam_practice.title: Transformaciones
exam_practice.instructions: Completa la segunda frase para que signifique lo mismo que la primera. Usa la palabra entre paréntesis sin cambiarla y entre dos y cinco palabras.

items.text: "The companies didn't plan carefully, so they are struggling now." → If the companies ___ (HAD) carefully, they wouldn't be struggling now.
items.explanation: Condicional mixto: pasado imposible (had planned) con consecuencia presente (wouldn't be).

items.text: "It is reported that the trial was a success." → The trial ___ (REPORTED) a success.
"She told her staff they could take Fridays off." → She ___ (LET) Fridays off.
"In the past, workers worked six days a week, but that isn't true now." → Workers ___ (USED) six days a week.
"The idea is very, very difficult to apply in a hospital." → The idea is ___ (EXTREMELY) to apply in a hospital.
"Small shops can't afford it. Big supermarkets can't afford it either." → Small shops can't afford it, and ___ (NEITHER).

vocabulary.definition: the amount of work or goods that a person or company produces
determined to do something without worrying about others' feelings
a person who doubts that something is true or will work
a group chosen by chance to represent a larger group
the total amount a company pays its workers
the difference between what something costs and what it sells for
to become or make something wider
to decide that something is not worth considering
